meaning: Each tie names the phrase of the paper that a Lean declaration states, as read side by side for Proof Reader (wcook04/proof-reader 79fe18157a1d, papers/contextual-embeddings). Titles, reading notes, topics and comparisons are AI-drafted or AI-assessed; no mathematician has reviewed them.

topics.name: Types and contexts
topics.description: Guest types and snoc contexts specify the types and available variables of the simply typed lambda calculus.

topics.name: Typed de Bruijn indices
topics.description: Top and Pop locate a variable of a given type within its context.

topics.name: First-order terms
topics.description: Variables, abstraction, application and the unit term form the first-order embedding.

topics.name: Singleton variable markers
topics.description: A singleton marker saves the context and type of the most recently introduced variable.

topics.name: Context extension
topics.description: The identity and extension instances recover a de Bruijn index from the binding and use contexts.

topics.name: Contextual terms
topics.description: Contextual terms use host functions for abstraction and reification for variable occurrences.

topics.name: Unembedding contextual terms
topics.description: Unembedding translates contextual syntax to first-order syntax while preserving context and guest type.

topics.name: Contextualising first-order terms
topics.description: Contextualisation translates first-order syntax back to contextual syntax.

topics.name: Converting individual variables
topics.description: An existential variable package separates conversion of indices from conversion of whole terms.

topics.name: Term round trips
topics.description: The two term equations express recovery of the original representation after both conversions.

topics.name: Index round trips
topics.description: The variable equations relate de Bruijn indices to their existential packages and support the term equations.

topics.name: Closed world assumption
topics.description: The reverse conversion relies on the assumption that reification uses only the identity and context-extension instances.

notes.Ctx: A context is either empty or an existing context extended by one guest type at the right. The final entry therefore describes the most recently introduced variable. The same contexts parameterise both term representations and their conversions, so the round-trip equations concern terms in an unchanged context, including contexts with free variables.
notes.Index: An index selects a variable of a specified guest type from a context. Top selects the last entry, while Pop passes over one later entry and keeps the selected variable’s type unchanged. Consequently an index cannot point outside its context or select an entry of the wrong type. These are typed positions, not arbitrary natural numbers.
notes.ProxyTop: The marker can refer only to the last entry of its saved context, and its guest type must equal that entry’s type. There is one possible marker at those fixed parameters. This prevents the illustrated choice between Top and Pop when inspecting the argument of a contextual abstraction. It does not by itself establish the round-trip theorem for complete contextual terms.
notes.ProxyVar: The paper’s existential variable package hides the binding context while retaining the variable’s guest type and its use context. Inside it are a top-variable marker and reification from the hidden context into the use context. This package lets conversion of an index be handled separately from conversion of a whole term. The reverse variable round trip recovers the package itself, not merely its reified index.
notes.ReifyIndex: Reification converts a saved top-variable marker into a typed index at the use context. The definition requires preservation of the variable’s guest type, but does not itself require the conversion to have been built from the two displayed instances. That additional restriction appears as the closed world assumption used for recovery of the original contextual representation.
notes.STLC: The first-order syntax contains variables, the unit term, abstractions and applications. An abstraction has a body in a context extended by the argument type; application requires its function and argument to have compatible types in the same context. These are exactly the constructors of Figure 1. The definition supplies syntax and typing, rather than an evaluator or a theorem about execution.
notes.STLCCtx: The contextual syntax has the same guest types and contexts as the first-order syntax. An abstraction receives a singleton marker for its newest variable, and a variable occurrence carries reification from that marker’s saved context into the occurrence’s context. Application and the unit term follow the usual typing rules. Recovering an identical contextual term after both conversions additionally uses the closed world assumption.
notes.Ty: The guest language has a unit type and function types. Every type is built from these two alternatives, so an expression such as $a\to b$ uses two already constructed guest types. This definition describes the small calculus in Section 2; it does not include the sum types, modal types or linear types discussed elsewhere in the paper.
notes.closedWorld: The assumption quantifies over every reification instance between two contexts. It says that the instance is either the identity-context case or one context-extension step built from another instance. It does not merely describe instances that a particular search has returned. The source assumes this condition; it contains no theorem deriving it from module encapsulation. The reverse variable and contextual term round trips depend on it.
notes.contextualise: Contextualisation translates a first-order term to a contextual term with the same context and guest type. In an abstraction, the newly supplied marker is ignored because variable occurrences already carry their de Bruijn indices. Each such index is converted separately to a contextual variable. This function is defined without the closed world assumption; the claim that both conversions are inverse functions uses the separate round-trip theorems.
notes.fromIndex: Conversion of an index proceeds by its Top and Pop cases. Top creates the package for the newest variable. Pop first converts the smaller index and then extends the resulting package’s use context by one type. Thus the result carries both a suitable saved binding context and reification back into the original index’s context, without requiring the closed world assumption.
notes.fromVar: This conversion injects the paper’s existential variable package into the full contextual term syntax. It reuses the package’s marker, hidden binding context and reification, so the resulting variable has exactly the same guest type and use context. No index traversal occurs here; the separate conversion from an index has already chosen the package’s contents.
notes.indexIsoL: For every typed de Bruijn index $i$, converting $i$ to its existential package and then applying the package’s reification recovers $i$. The statement quantifies over arbitrary contexts and guest types. Its proof follows the Top and Pop cases of the index, and does not use the closed world assumption. This is the variable fact needed for the first-order term round trip.
notes.indexIsoR: Begin with a saved variable marker and its reification into a use context. Reifying the marker and converting the resulting index back yields the original existential variable package. This recovers the package, including its hidden-context information, rather than only an equal index. The proof uses the closed world assumption to reduce every reification to the identity or extension case, then continues through the smaller use context.
notes.instReifyIndexRefl: When the binding context and use context coincide, reification sends the saved marker to Top. No later variable needs to be crossed. This is the base case used when constructing the variable package for a Top index, and it is one of the two allowed cases in the closed world assumption.
notes.instReifyIndexSnoc: Suppose reification is available from a binding context into a use context. Extending the use context by one guest type produces another reification by applying Pop to the previous result. The formal definition places this extended context directly in the instance head. It therefore shares the paper’s reification equation but does not reproduce the Haskell technique of deferring the context-shape equality until after instance selection.
notes.isoL: For every first-order term $e$, in any context and at any guest type, $\operatorname{unembed}(\operatorname{contextualise}(e))=e$. No closed world assumption is used in this direction: contextualisation itself constructs the reification instances needed to recover each original index. The proof proceeds through the term’s constructors, using the first index round trip in the variable case. This is one half of the claimed isomorphism.
notes.isoR: For every contextual term $e$, $\operatorname{contextualise}(\operatorname{unembed}(e))=e$, assuming the closed world condition on reification instances. The variable case uses recovery of the original existential package; the abstraction case uses function extensionality and the singleton marker. Together with the first-order round trip, this supplies the isomorphism under the assumption explicitly discussed in Section 3.3. It does not establish that module encapsulation enforces that assumption.
notes.toCVar: The equation $\operatorname{toCVar}=\operatorname{fromVar}\circ\operatorname{fromIndex}$ gives the variable branch of contextualisation. First package the index, then turn that package into a contextual variable. Both steps preserve the variable’s guest type and use context. The index round-trip theorem explains why unembedding recovers the original index.
notes.unembed: Unembedding maps a contextual term to a first-order term in the same context and of the same guest type. Variables are converted with their stored reification; an abstraction’s function is applied to the unique marker for its new variable. Applications and the unit term are translated recursively. This conversion is defined without the closed world assumption, which is needed only for one of the round-trip proofs.
notes.varTop: The newest-variable package uses the current nonempty context as both binding context and use context. Its marker identifies the last entry, and its reification is the identity-context instance, which returns Top. This is the base case for converting an index into a package. The guest type is arbitrary, provided it is the type of that final context entry.
notes.weakenPVar: Weakening extends the use context by one type while keeping the saved binding context and marker unchanged. It also replaces the stored reification with the extension instance, so reifying the weakened package adds one Pop. The apparently unchanged package on both sides of the paper’s equation therefore has a different use context and a correspondingly extended reification.
